blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better buy for pure residential volume: at 100 GB it costs about $200 ($2/GB), and from a terabyte it drops to $0.90/GB, cheaper than ProxyEmpire's $1.50/GB at the same level. ProxyEmpire is the better choice when you need SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential gateway is HTTP(S) only), ISP-level targeting, sticky sessions for account work, or rotating mobile IPs from the same account. Both keep unused traffic, so irregular usage is safe with either.

Rayobyte and ProxyEmpire share a rare and valuable policy: residential traffic you pay for does not expire. That takes the usual use-it-or-lose-it worry off the table and turns this into a comparison of price curves, protocol support and product range. Rayobyte gets dramatically cheaper as volume grows and has deep datacenter roots. ProxyEmpire adds free ISP targeting, SOCKS5, 24-hour sticky sessions and mobile proxies on the same system. Here is which one fits which buyer.

blocks.text: Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire sells residential, mobile, static residential and datacenter proxies from one dashboard and competes on flexibility. Traffic you prepay never expires, ISP-level targeting is free, and the $1.97 trial lets you test both residential and mobile networks before committing. Its 30M+ advertised pool is smaller on paper than the enterprise providers, but independent testing has rated its real reachable pool well relative to its claims.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: Rayobyte vs ProxyEmpire
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

At 10 GB a month the two cost almost the same: about $35 with Rayobyte against $35 with ProxyEmpire. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; Rayobyte comes to about $200. Neither provider makes you use it or lose it: both Rayobyte and ProxyEmpire let unused traffic carry forward, so the comparison really comes down to rate and features.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published' and ProxyEmpire lists '30M+'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Rayobyte lists Global countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, Rayobyte offers country, region and city, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. ProxyEmpire supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in ProxyEmpire's favour. On sessions, Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available, and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. With ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. Run the same small test on both before committing.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. With ProxyEmpire: Google was its weakest target in independent tests. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. How Rayobyte compares: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. ProxyEmpire: free city and ISP targeting. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. How Rayobyte compares: fewer carrier or ASN controls.

Tight budgets: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Rayobyte: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. ProxyEmpire: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Rayobyte: Check current offer. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Rayobyte and ProxyEmpire before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Rayobyte vs ProxyEmpire faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Rayobyte: check current offer; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Rayobyte comes out ahead in 0, ProxyEmpire in 2, and 4 are ties. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
